stories.headline: U.S. Supreme Court ruling on Trump mail-voting order creates uncertainty for Colorado elections
stories.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court's decision Monday unblocking President Trump's executive order restricting mail voting has raised significant questions for Colorado, where the vast majority of voters receive ballots by mail. The court ruled that Democratic states, including Colorado, filed their legal challenges too early because the order's directives had not yet taken effect, but did not rule on the merits of the challenges.

Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold said nothing has changed for now, as a second court order stemming from a League of Women Voters lawsuit remains in place barring implementation of Postal Service changes required by Trump's order. Griswold said further litigation is expected once those USPS changes take effect this week.

On Wednesday, Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser joined dozens of other states in filing a new lawsuit to block the executive order's postal service provisions. Weiser had signaled the move Monday, saying the Supreme Court 'may have dodged the merits' but that the claims would 'have their day in court.'

County clerks across Colorado are already preparing to mail ballots to military and overseas voters, with general mail ballots set to go out in early October. Griswold acknowledged that if legal challenges are not resolved quickly, there may simply not be enough time for the executive order to be fully implemented before Election Day.

stories.headline: Colorado voters to decide mail ballot ID requirement after Initiative 362 qualifies for November ballot
stories.summary:
Colorado voters will be asked in November whether to amend the state constitution to require people to verify their identity when submitting mail ballots by including the last four digits of their Social Security number or their full driver's license or state ID number. The Colorado Secretary of State's Office confirmed Wednesday that supporters of Initiative 362 turned in a sufficient number of voter signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot.

The initiative was filed by Chuck Broerman, a Republican and former top elections official in El Paso County, and Suzanne Taheri, a Republican who previously served as Colorado's deputy secretary of state. The effort was funded largely by $2.2 million from the Coalition for American Prosperity and Growth, a group registered to a Colorado Springs mailbox store whose ultimate donors are not publicly disclosed.

Supporters argue the measure would help ensure voters are only submitting ballots that belong to them. Opponents contend Colorado's existing signature verification system is already secure and that adding identification requirements would create unnecessary barriers and lead to more ballots being rejected.

Because Initiative 362 would amend the state constitution, it must receive support from at least 55% of voters to pass. It will be among as many as 14 measures on the statewide ballot this fall.

stories.headline: Gov. Polis grants pardons to 29 Coloradans convicted of theft, drug and fraud offenses
stories.summary:
Gov. Jared Polis on Wednesday granted pardons to 29 Coloradans convicted of a range of crimes including theft, drug possession and fraud. Twenty-eight of the individuals had pleaded guilty to their offenses and one had been convicted at trial, according to pardon letters released by the governor's office.

In letters to the recipients, Polis wrote that each had been selected from hundreds of applicants and had demonstrated a commitment to moving past their convictions, citing accomplishments such as raising children, pursuing higher education, serving in the military and excelling in their careers.

The governor is the only official who can grant clemency for state crimes under the Colorado Constitution. To date, Polis has granted 165 individual pardons and 35 commutations, in addition to more than 4,000 blanket pardons for marijuana and psilocybin-related possession offenses.

The announcement comes months after Polis drew significant controversy by granting clemency to former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters, who had been serving a nine-year sentence. That decision prompted backlash from elected officials and the Colorado Democratic Party, and led to the firing of two clemency board members who publicly objected.

stories.headline: Third-party candidates mount long-shot bids across Colorado in 2026 election cycle
stories.summary:
Dozens of independent and third-party candidates are running for offices up and down the ballot in Colorado this fall, even as history suggests major-party candidates will dominate the results. The 2026 cycle features candidates from the Forward Party, Unity Party and other minor parties recognized by the state, with races ranging from U.S. Senate to local offices.

Bob Chew, a former registered Republican running for U.S. Senate under the Forward Party line, has invested more than $1 million of his own money in his campaign and reserved $1.3 million in television advertising through September. He argues that with more than half of Colorado's roughly 4 million active registered voters unaffiliated with either major party, there is an opening for a serious third-party candidacy on issues such as the national debt.

Other minor-party candidates have far fewer resources. Adam Withrow of Walsenburg, who ran for Congress under the Unity Party in the last cycle, received just over 2,700 votes in the sprawling 3rd Congressional District — far short of the winning total but more than he expected.

The major-party U.S. Senate candidates this cycle are Democratic incumbent John Hickenlooper and Republican state Sen. Mark Baisley. Minor party candidates qualify for the ballot through party conventions, while unaffiliated candidates must collect signatures based on the office sought.

stories.headline: Most Colorado universities undecided on whether to respond to Trump administration's free speech questionnaire
stories.summary:
Most Colorado colleges and universities have not decided whether to respond to a questionnaire sent earlier this month by U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon asking institutions to detail their policies on free speech, research, admissions and campus protests. At least one Colorado university has said it does not intend to answer the letter.

Colorado's two largest public university systems said Wednesday they are still evaluating the request. McMahon's Aug. 3 letter asks institutions to post their answers prominently on their websites by year's end, but does not include explicit threats related to funding or federal investigations, distinguishing it from some earlier Trump administration actions targeting higher education.

The letter represents the latest effort by the Trump administration to shape campus policy nationally, arriving at a time when public confidence in higher education is broadly declining. Questions in the letter address issues typically decided at the campus level by administrators and faculty.

Colorado's colleges are navigating the request carefully given the broader context of federal pressure on universities. Officials have not said publicly what factors are guiding their deliberations on whether or how to respond.

stories.headline: Missing endangered 13-year-old girl last seen in north Denver, CBI issues alert
stories.summary:
The Colorado Bureau of Investigation issued an endangered missing person alert Wednesday for a 13-year-old girl last seen in north Denver more than a week ago. Jody Hunt was last seen on foot in the 3100 block of Hooker Street at 8 a.m. on Aug. 20, according to the CBI.

Hunt is described as white, 5 feet 2 inches tall and 100 pounds with brown hair and brown eyes. She was last seen wearing a gray hoodie, black sweatpants and purple Crocs. The CBI characterized her as a high-risk missing juvenile.

The Adams County Sheriff's Office is leading the investigation. Anyone with information about Hunt's whereabouts is asked to call 911 or the Adams County Sheriff's Office at 303-288-1535.

stories.headline: Colorado inmate who lost leg at CoreCivic prison sues over denied medical care
stories.summary:
A Colorado inmate who had his leg amputated after being held for four days without adequate treatment at a private prison in southern Colorado has filed a federal negligence lawsuit. Paul Knuth first reported debilitating pain in his right foot on June 23, 2025, while incarcerated at the Bent County Correctional Facility in Las Animas, but was not sent to a hospital for four days, according to the lawsuit filed Monday in U.S. District Court.

Doctors ultimately diagnosed Knuth with MRSA, a potentially fatal bacterial infection, and amputated his leg to save his life. The lawsuit alleges that a nurse accused Knuth of faking illness on two separate occasions despite lab results indicating infection, and that medical staff failed to order antibiotics or rapid-screening tests despite escalating symptoms.

The lawsuit names as defendants the nurse, a physician assistant, CoreCivic — the private company that operates the facility — and the Bent County Board of Commissioners, which contracted with CoreCivic. It alleges negligence and violations of Knuth's Eighth Amendment rights. The suit further claims CoreCivic chronically understaffs its facilities and that Bent County was assessed more than $162,000 in damages for staffing deficiencies at the prison in 2025 alone.

Bent County commissioners did not respond to requests for comment. The lawsuit states that after additional surgeries and weeks of rehabilitation, Knuth was returned to prison with a permanent disability caused by 'an eminently treatable infection that was ignored until it nearly killed him.'

stories.headline: Severe thunderstorms bring large hail and high winds to Denver metro area
stories.summary:
The National Weather Service issued a severe thunderstorm warning for metro Denver on Wednesday evening, with storms threatening winds up to 60 mph and quarter-sized hail. A storm near Wheat Ridge moved east toward Denver, prompting warnings of hail damage to vehicles and wind damage to roofs, siding and trees.

The warning covered a broad swath of the metro area including Arvada, Aurora, Denver, Englewood, Golden, Greenwood Village, Highlands Ranch, Lakewood, Littleton, Thornton, Westminster and Wheat Ridge, among other communities. A separate severe thunderstorm watch had been active since earlier in the day for the Front Range and most of the eastern plains, extending into Nebraska and Wyoming.

Forecasters warned that heavy rain accompanying the storms could trigger flash flooding in southern Colorado, particularly in wildfire burn scars. A flash flood watch was issued for the Aspen Acres burn scar in Pueblo County, where fire-damaged soils are especially prone to runoff.

stories.headline: Bears invade Denver-area school campuses as drought drives animals into suburbs
stories.summary:
Schools across Denver's suburbs have issued unusual warnings to students and parents this fall: watch out for bears. Cherry Creek Schools and Jeffco Public Schools have each placed multiple campuses on secure status — prohibiting students from leaving buildings — due to bear sightings near schools in Greenwood Village, Centennial, Arvada and Littleton since classes resumed last week.

Wildlife biologists say a widespread drought has depleted the berries, acorns and other plants bears typically feed on at higher elevations, pushing the animals into urban areas in search of food. Bears are also in a pre-hibernation feeding frenzy typical of late summer, compounding the problem. Statewide, Colorado has recorded nearly double the number of bear encounters compared to the same period last year.

Cherry Creek Schools spokeswoman Abbe Smith said bears venturing as far as Greenwood Village and Centennial is 'not normal.' On the first day of classes Aug. 17, at least four Cherry Creek schools were placed on secure status after a bear was spotted at Tommy Davis Park in Greenwood Village. A bear spotted near Sierra Elementary in Arvada and another near Governor's Ranch Elementary in Littleton prompted additional family notifications this week.

Cassandre Venumiere-Lefebvre, a wildlife biologist at Colorado State University, said bears are 'particularly desperate because of the drought' and that their presence this far into urban areas is highly unusual. Districts are notifying parents so they can adjust pickup arrangements for students who normally walk home.

stories.headline: Colorado wolf packs remain in northwest region as spring pups begin to explore
stories.summary:
Colorado's collared wolf packs continued to occupy the northwest part of the state over the past month, with their territory ranging generally from Gunnison to Vail and Meeker, according to a map released Wednesday by Colorado Parks and Wildlife. The wolves' range changed little from the previous month.

Pups born this spring have begun traveling short distances with other pack members and are now approximately four months old. CPW biologists are monitoring four reproducing packs and working to determine how many pups each pack added this season. Average wolf litters contain four to six pups.

The update provides the latest snapshot of Colorado's wolf reintroduction program, which has been closely watched by ranchers, conservationists and wildlife managers since gray wolves were reintroduced to the state.

stories.headline: Denver-based developer preserved 120 affordable apartments in Eagle, averting displacement of dozens of families
stories.summary:
A Denver-based affordable housing developer stepped in to save a 120-unit apartment complex in the mountain town of Eagle from conversion to market-rate housing, preserving below-market rents for families who had few other options in the high-cost resort community. Ulysses Development Group acquired Eagle Villas in 2024 as affordability restrictions on the 1990s-era complex were nearing expiration and the property had been listed for sale on the open market.

Working with the Eagle County Housing and Development Authority and the state, UDG assembled a financing package to keep rents restricted for households earning roughly 45% to 60% of the area median income — between about $62,400 and $83,200 annually for a family of four — and to renovate all 120 units. Eagle Villas is the largest income-restricted housing complex in the town of Eagle.

The deal highlights a growing but underappreciated challenge in affordable housing: complexes built with federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits carry affordability restrictions that expire, after which owners can convert properties to market-rate rentals or sell them to developers who will. Eagle County resiliency director Tori Franks said the cost of losing low-income units in high-cost communities extends well beyond housing, including job loss, school disruptions and the erosion of social networks.

Residents like Julieth Kennedy, a mother of five who had begun searching for apartments in Aurora when the sale was announced, said the acquisition kept her family close to relatives who provide childcare and allowed her children to remain in their school. 'It would have been depressing for them,' she said of a potential move.

stories.headline: Rockies rout Nationals 13-1 in Washington, snapping recent home-loss franchise record streak
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies defeated the Washington Nationals 13-1 on Wednesday night in Washington, posting a lopsided road victory fueled by four home runs and 15 hits. Connor Norby led the offense with a grand slam and five RBI, while Troy Johnston, Cole Carrigg and Hunter Goodman also homered for Colorado.

The victory came one day after the Rockies set a franchise record with their ninth consecutive home loss at Coors Field, completing a sweep at the hands of the Cleveland Guardians. Wednesday's win was a sharp offensive turnaround for a team that has struggled throughout the 2026 season.

Norby finished 2-for-4 with two runs scored in addition to his five RBI. TJ Rumfield reached base safely four times on two hits and two walks. The Rockies sent 11 batters to the plate in an eight-run eighth inning that effectively ended any doubt about the outcome.

joke.joke: Whenever I'm in a hotel and I hear someone in the next room, I always think, 'I hope they can't hear me eating.'

topStory.headline: NDAs Shield Data Center Deals From Public as Opposition Grows Across Party Lines
topStory.summary:
Technology companies negotiating data center projects with local governments across the United States are routinely requiring elected officials to sign nondisclosure agreements, keeping terms of major development deals hidden from the public. Records requests filed by the Gulf States Newsroom and Type Investigations uncovered at least 54 NDAs signed by Louisiana officials since Gov. Jeff Landry took office in early 2024, including agreements covering data center projects in Rapides Parish, where Dallas-based Applied Digital Corp. is breaking ground on a 300-acre facility near the town of Boyce.

Residents near affected sites say the secrecy has fueled distrust of local leaders and left basic questions unanswered. Foster Hensel, a beekeeper in central Louisiana who farms near the Boyce construction site, said he worries about rising utility bills and environmental changes, and questioned why negotiations were conducted behind closed doors. University of Virginia researcher Eric Bonds, who surveyed 31 data center projects in Virginia, found NDAs were used in at least 25 of them, calling the practice 'standard.' David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, said companies use information control to gain a negotiating advantage as they move from jurisdiction to jurisdiction seeking the most favorable terms.

Opposition to rapid data center expansion has emerged as one of the few genuinely bipartisan issues in contemporary American politics, drawing together conservative farmers, environmental groups and rural residents across Republican-leaning Nebraska, Texas and Wyoming, swing-state Pennsylvania and Democratic-leaning New Mexico. In Cass County, Nebraska, officials approved a 12-month moratorium on data center development after residents packed a firehouse meeting in the village of Murdock to voice concerns about farmland loss, water depletion and higher electricity costs. Energy company Tenaska has been exploring options on more than 1,300 acres along Highway 75 in the county for a project that could include a data center and a natural gas power plant.

Legislative pushback against NDA use is accelerating at the state level. Bills to ban the agreements on data center projects have been introduced in Michigan, Oklahoma, Kentucky and Ohio, and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro last week prohibited their use on data center projects overseen by agencies under his authority. Supporters of data center expansion, including President Donald Trump and some labor union leaders, argue the projects deliver jobs and economic investment while advancing U.S. technological competition with China, but critics say the pace and secrecy of development are outrunning communities' ability to respond.
